In 2016, the plastic-shed vegetable production planting acreage in China reached 3.92 million hectares, which is approximately 20 % of the total vegetable acreage in the country (CSB, 2017; Li et al., 2018a). This enabled the average annual supply of fresh vegetables to reach 378 kg per capita, which is much greater than the global average of 143 kg per capita (FAO, 2020). Plastic-shed vegetable production is characterized by an extremely high input of irrigation water and fertilizers (Yao et al., 2019). Typical irrigation rates in plastic-shed vegetable production range from 620 to 1180 mm per vegetable season (Lv et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2019), with an average of 50–120 mm per irrigation event (He et al., 2009; Lv et al., 2019). This is approximately 2–7 times higher than irrigation rates for cereal crops in the same region of China (Xin and Tao, 2020), where most solar plastic-shed vegetable production is located. Similarly, annual fertilizer nitrogen (N) input in typical plastic-shed vegetable fields (two crop seasons per year) reached 3338 kg ha−1 in Shouguang County, China, approximately 6–14 times that in local wheat-maize rotations (Liu et al., 2014). Compared with cereals, vegetables have lower nutrient uptake because of their shallow root system and low quantity of harvested dry matter (Min et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018). Min et al. (2012) and Liang et al. (2015) found that N use efficiency (NUE) was only 18 % and 9.5 % in a plastic-shed tomato system, respectively, which was significantly lower than the NUE of the main grain systems (29 %–45 %) in Northern China (Chuan et al., 2010; Li et al., 2015a; Yu and Shi, 2015). Although it is not always appropriate to compare vegetable and cereal crops, these findings indicate there is room to improve the NUE for vegetable production to an acceptable level (e.g., 40 %; Zhu and Chen, 2002). With the intensification and popularization of plastic-shed vegetable production in China, the negative environmental impacts of conventional planting methods have gradually become prominent. Surplus nutrients either remain in the soil (Bai et al., 2020), or are lost to the environment via various pathways, including N2O, NO, N2 (Yao et al., 2019), NH3 (Zhang et al., 2019a), and N leaching (Lv et al., 2019). N2O emissions from plastic-shed fields account for approximately 25 % of total farmland N2O emissions in China (Yao et al., 2019). Plastic-sheds are characterized by a close inner environment with high soil temperature and moisture (Han et al., 2017), which significantly affects soil properties (Ding et al., 2019; Lv et al., 2020), promotes soil microbial activity, and increases N2O emissions (Duan et al., 2019a; Ye et al., 2018). Previous studies found that N2O emissions for plastic-shed production increase with increasing fertilizer N rates (Chen et al., 2014; Cui et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018), and their relationships vary among crops (Chen et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018) and regions (Liyanage et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018) because of variations in climate (Aliyu et al., 2018), soil (Gu et al., 2020), vegetable species (Yang et al., 2019), and farming measures (Wu et al., 2020). Compared with leafy vegetables, fruit vegetables with a longer growth period require higher N levels and more irrigation, and therefore take up more N (Luo et al., 2015; Min et al., 2012; Yao et al., 2019). Fertilizer type significantly influences N2O emissions (Shcherbak et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017). Farmers commonly apply synthetic fertilizer in combination with composted animal manure in Chinese vegetable production (Wang et al., 2018), to meet the crop N demand (Tang et al., 2019), and simultaneously improve the soil organic matter (SOM) and ameliorate negative soil properties (Chen et al., 2020). Recent studies indicated that partial replacement of synthetic N with manure was optimal for mitigating N2O emissions from farmland (Chang et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2018a), either because of slow N release from manure (Ding et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2019a) or stimulated denitrification (Meijide et al., 2007; Duan et al., 2019b). However, some studies have shown that a combination of synthetic N fertilizer and manure emitted more N2O at the same N application rate compared with synthetic fertilizer alone (Dong et al., 2007; Hao et al., 2012). This is because the combination of synthetic fertilizer with manure simultaneously inputs carbon and N, increasing the nitrification and denitrification rates and subsequently increasing N2O emissions (Aguilera et al., 2013). However, Charles et al. (2017) and Wang et al. (2018) found that a mixed application of synthetic fertilizer and manure did not influence N2O emissions and emission factors (EFs), compared with synthetic N fertilizer alone in plastic-shed soils. In addition to fertilization, other measures such as the irrigation water quantity (Yao et al., 2019), nitrification inhibitors (Wu et al., 2018b; Zhao et al., 2017), and soil properties (Ding et al., 2019) have also been reported to significantly affect N2O emissions in plastic-shed vegetable production. However, because of the limited amount of published research on this topic, or because a mixture of farming measures such as flood and drip irrigation are compared, there have been conflicting findings among meta-data studies (Gu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2019). Department of Soil Science, University of Eldoret, Eldoret, Kenya * See more Article metrics View details Abstract Nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from cropland soils are a significant source of greenhouse gases in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), yet fluxes and drivers remain poorly quantified. This review synthesizes findings from 39 field-based studies across Sub-Saharan Africa to assess current knowledge, key drivers, and research gaps. Additionally, this review offers a focused analysis on the effect of nitrogen fertilizer application on N2O emissions. The main finding is that emissions were strongly influenced by nitrogen input rates, precipitation, cropping systems, soil types, and measurement durations. Emission factors often diverge from IPCC Tier 1 defaults, suggesting the need for context-specific values. However, research is unevenly distributed: Studies from Kenya dominate the literature, while large areas, especially in Central Africa, lack data. Methodological inconsistencies further limit comparability across studies. We identify priorities for future research, including geographic expansion, standardized protocols, and improved integration of climate and agronomic variables. Strengthening the regional evidence base is essential for accurate inventories and for developing climate-smart agricultural policies tailored to SSA’s diverse agroecosystems. 1 Introduction Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a potent greenhouse gas (GHG), with a global warming potential (GWP) approximately 273 times greater than carbon dioxide (CO2) over a 100-year period (Intergovernmental Panel On Climate Change, 2023) and it is currently the most important ozone-depleting gas (Ravishankara et al., 2009). In soils, N2O is primarily produced through two biological processes, nitrification and denitrification, with nitrification depending on ammonium NH4+ and oxygen (O2) availability, while denitrification depends on nitrate (NO3−), degradable organic matter, and O2 limitation. These processes are mainly controlled by soil properties, agricultural management practices, microbial communities and environmental conditions such as soil moisture and temperature and the availability of organic carbon and nitrogen (N) in the soil (Butterbach-Bahl et al., 2013; Della Chiesa et al., 2019; Cui et al., 2024; Piñeiro-Guerra et al., 2025). Regional evidence and context for sub-Saharan African soils

The available evidence shows that SSA cropland N2O research is still unevenly distributed and relatively limited in scope, but it does support the existence of regional studies and syntheses focused on the region. A recent Frontiers review explicitly synthesizes findings from 39 field-based studies across Sub-Saharan Africa and emphasizes that the literature is dominated by Kenya, while much of Central Africa lacks data [N2-F2]. This regional synthesis is the strongest direct evidence here that SSA has a growing body of studies on cropland N2O emissions, even if the coverage is incomplete.

On soil types, crop systems, and management practices, the review notes that emissions were strongly influenced by nitrogen input rates, precipitation, cropping systems, soil types, and measurement durations [N2-F2]. It also identifies the need to understand N cycling and emission hotspots in pastoral livestock systems in SSA [N2-R4], which expands the regional context beyond croplands to include livestock-related N inputs. In the broader SSA climate and land-use context, the evidence indicates that temperature, soil moisture, rainfall, and fertilizer use are the main drivers influencing N2O emissions [N5-F3]. Another source reports that wetting of seasonally dry African soils caused nitric oxide emissions to increase by more than an order of magnitude, while SSA N2O emissions are also linked to land-use changes associated with loss of biomass and soil organic carbon [N5-R1][N5-R4]. These findings suggest that SSA soils are shaped by a combination of dry-season moisture limitation, seasonal wetting events, and land-use intensity.

In terms of how SSA patterns differ from global or temperate datasets, the review notes that emission factors often diverge from IPCC Tier 1 defaults and that SSA research is unevenly distributed [N2-F2]. This implies that SSA emissions are not simply a direct extrapolation of global or temperate studies; they are context-specific and require regionally adapted values. The review also highlights that SSA cropland N2O emissions are projected to rise with increasing use of resource inputs, especially N fertilizers and organic amendments [N2-F2], which aligns with a broader global trend of nonlinearity in N2O responses to inputs but emphasizes the regional importance of fertilizer use in SSA.

Regarding whether SSA studies specifically report dose-response or only overall emission trends, the evidence is mixed. The Frontiers review explicitly says it offers a focused analysis of the effect of nitrogen fertilizer application on N2O emissions and that emissions were strongly influenced by nitrogen input rates [N2-F2]. This is direct evidence that SSA studies do report dose-response-like findings. However, the review also notes that studies are unevenly distributed and that methodological inconsistencies limit comparability across studies [N2-F2], so some SSA studies may only contribute overall emission trends rather than precise dose-response curves. The additional SSA-specific evidence is more descriptive than dose-response-oriented: it identifies fertilizer use as a main driver [N5-F3] and reports a strong response of emissions to residue retention in conservation agriculture [N2-R2]. Overall, the regional evidence base is growing but remains uneven, and SSA studies do support dose-response interpretation, especially for fertilizer inputs, while broader land-use and climate drivers also shape observed patterns [N2-F2][N5-F3].

Limitations and caveats in interpreting the evidence

The evidence indicates several important limitations that weaken claims of a universal exponential relationship in SSA soils. First, measurement and sampling constraints are a major issue. The Frontiers review notes that methodological inconsistencies further limit comparability across studies [N2-F2], and the general evidence from SSA N2O research shows that the literature is unevenly distributed, with Kenya dominating and large areas of Central Africa lacking data [N2-F2]. This unevenness means that many observed relationships may reflect sampling bias rather than a true regional pattern. The same review also states that emission factors often diverge from IPCC Tier 1 defaults, suggesting that regional variability is substantial and that generalizations from SSA data should be cautious [N2-F2].

Confounding variables such as moisture, temperature, and crop residue are also central. The SSA synthesis identifies temperature, soil moisture, rainfall, and fertilizer use as main drivers of N2O emissions [N5-F3]. Another source reports that wetting of seasonally dry African soils caused nitric oxide emissions to increase by more than an order of magnitude [N5-R1], while conservation agriculture with residue retention increased soil NO3-N and N2O emissions compared to conventional practices [N2-R2]. These findings show that moisture and residue management can strongly influence observed emission responses, making it difficult to isolate nitrogen inputs as the sole driver. The review also notes that measurement durations affect emissions [N2-F2], which implies that short-term or seasonal measurements may miss long-term or episodic responses.

Generalizability is another key limitation. The SSA literature is unevenly distributed, and many studies are concentrated in Kenya, while large parts of Central Africa lack data [N2-F2]. The review also emphasizes that methodological inconsistencies limit comparability [N2-F2], which means that findings from one SSA site may not apply to another. The broader climate and land-use evidence further suggests that SSA emissions are shaped by land-use changes, biomass loss, and soil organic carbon dynamics [N5-R4], so results from one SSA cropping system may not generalize to pastoral systems, drylands, or other land uses [N2-R4]. Finally, the evidence supports dose-response interpretation, but the studies in SSA are not always strong enough to justify it confidently. The review notes that findings are uneven and methodologically inconsistent [N2-F2], while the SSA N2O literature also includes observational studies and small-sample comparisons [N5-R1][N2-R2]. This means that dose-response conclusions should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive, especially when studies are observational or have limited sample sizes [N5-R1][N2-F2].

Direct evidence supporting an exponential or nonlinear relationship between nitrogen inputs and N₂O emissions

The evidence from the direct search material is strongest for an exponential or nonlinear relationship when nitrogen inputs exceed crop demand. The Frontiers review explicitly says that emissions were strongly influenced by nitrogen input rates and that emission factors often diverge from IPCC Tier 1 defaults [N2-F2]. It also notes that cropland N2O emissions in SSA are projected to rise with increasing use of N fertilizers and organic amendments [N2-F2], which is consistent with a nonlinear response to inputs. However, the direct evidence for exponential behavior comes more clearly from the broader agricultural literature rather than from a single SSA study.

The strongest direct evidence for an exponential or nonlinear relationship is in the global and temperate literature. One source states that an exponential increase in N2O emissions was found when N input exceeded crop demand [N1-R1]. Another meta-analysis reports that the N2O response to N inputs grew significantly faster than linear for synthetic fertilizers and for most crop types [N1-R3]. A related PNAS paper similarly found a general trend of exponentially increasing N2O emissions as N inputs increase to exceed crop needs [N1-R4]. These are the clearest supports for an exponential or nonlinear dose-response pattern. A meta-analysis of soil background N2O emissions also notes that N2O emissions on fertilizer nitrogen input were studied, and the broader literature shows that N2O emissions increase with N application [N1-R2].

The evidence also includes model-based or fitted curves that suggest exponential or sigmoidal behavior. The KBS LTER source explicitly tests the hypothesis that N2O emissions respond exponentially to fertilizer N in semi-arid, sub-tropical irrigated agriculture [N6-R2]. Another source reports that cumulative N2O emissions increased exponentially with N fertilizer rates in a tropical sugarcane cropping system, with emissions ranging from 0.29 to 3.06 kg N ha⁻¹ and emission factors ranging from 0.69 to 1.11% [N6-R4]. These fitted exponential responses are strong direct evidence that the relationship is not strictly linear. The search material also mentions an exponential relationship between N2O emission and fertilizer nitrogen input, with supporting evidence from a systematic analysis in China [N1-R1][N1-F1], which further reinforces the existence of exponential or nonlinear behavior under high N inputs.

Thresholds or inflection points where linearity breaks are also supported by the evidence. The Frontiers review notes that emissions were strongly influenced by nitrogen input rates [N2-F2], and the global literature indicates that N2O emissions increase more rapidly when inputs exceed crop demand [N1-R1]. The sugarcane study reports exponential increases as N fertilizer rates rise, which implies an inflection point at which the response becomes nonlinear [N6-R4]. The PNAS and KBS LTER evidence also suggest that responses are not constant across all N inputs but change with the amount of fertilizer applied [N1-R3][N6-R2]. This is consistent with a threshold or nonlinear regime rather than a simple linear relationship.

Evidence from synthetic fertilizer, organic amendment, or crop-type comparisons is present, though it is less abundant in the SSA-specific material provided here. The SSA synthesis notes that emissions were influenced by nitrogen input rates and fertilizer use [N2-F2], while the broader literature shows that fertilizer type significantly influences N2O emissions [N1-F1]. The synthetic fertilizer and manure comparisons in the China study indicate that partial replacement of synthetic N with manure can be optimal for mitigating N2O emissions, but combinations can also increase emissions due to simultaneous carbon and nitrogen inputs [N1-F1]. This is relevant because it shows that N2O responses vary by input type, not just by quantity. The crop-type evidence is also present: the KBS LTER source notes that responses vary among crops in semi-arid, sub-tropical irrigated agriculture [N6-R2], while the China study reports that responses vary among crops and regions [N1-F1]. This supports the broader conclusion that the relationship is nonlinear and context-dependent.

Overall, the direct evidence is mixed in that the strongest exponential and nonlinear support comes from global and temperate studies rather than a single SSA study. However, the evidence does clearly indicate that N2O emissions rise more rapidly at higher nitrogen inputs, especially when inputs exceed crop demand, and that fitted exponential or sigmoidal behavior is plausible in both global and SSA-related contexts [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R4]. The evidence therefore supports an exponential or nonlinear relationship, but it does not establish a universal SSA-only exponential pattern [N1-R1][N2-F2].
